newsitem.title: DUBAI: Coalition forces complete relocation in Saudi.
newsitem.headline: Coalition forces complete relocation in Saudi.

text.p: U.S.-led coalition troops enforcing a "no-fly zone" over southern Iraq from Saudi Arabia have moved to a new base as part of a plan to improve their security in the kingdom, a U.S. spokesman said on Thursday.
"All the aircraft have been moved...As well as 3,000 troops. The relocation is completed," said Lieutenant-Colonel Andrew Bourland, public affairs director for the Joint Task Force Southwest Asia.

He said the move to the remote Prince Sultan Base at al-Kharj, 100 km (60 miles) southeast of the capital Riyadh, was completed earlier this month, but that work will continue on improving security measures for the mainly U.S. forces.
The headquarters of the task force, which also includes British and French troops, had moved in August to another base south of Riyadh.
The shift was prompted by two deadly bomb attacks targeting U.S. forces in the oil-rich state in the past year.

A huge fuel truck ripped through a U.S. housing complex in Khobar in June, killing 19 American airmen. Last November, a bomb at a U.S.-run military training centre in Riyadh killed five Americans and two Indians.
More threats against Americans in the kingdom have been received since the last attack. Up to 40,000 Americans live and work in the kingdom.
The move, which the Pentagon has said will cost about $200 million to be shared equally with Saudi Arabia, allows for the relocation of 4,000 to 5,000 troops from Dhahran and Riyadh to the air base.
"Over the coming months the number (of relocated troops) may grow...We have taken a number of force protection measures to ensure the safety of the forces," Bourland said.
He said there was capacity to expand the number of relocated troops to 6,000.

A Pentagon report, ordered by Defence Secretary William Perry, said in September that commanders failed to provide adequate protection for the Khobar post despite evidence it had become a "potential terrorist target".
A Lebanese newspaper close to Saudi circles reported on Thursday that Saudi authorities had arrested 11 people in connection with the June blast in Khobar.
Al-Bayrak said in a frontpage report that the detainees were "being interrogated minutely and in utmost secrecy."

U.S. officials in Saudi Arabia said that Federal Bureau of Investigation officials continued to work with Saudi officials on the investigation into the June bombing, but that any announcements on arrests would be made by Saudi authorities.
There was no immediate Saudi reaction to the report.
The newspaper said there was a link between the 11 suspects and "elements" behind the Riyadh bombing. Four Saudis who confessed on state television to carrying it out were executed.
